(1) Enhanced Zonal Analysis Procedure (EZAP) and associated Electrical Wiring Interconnection
 System (EWIS)
 (a) Enhanced Zonal Analysis Procedure (EZAP) is an analytical procedure required by Part
 25, Appendix H, Section H25.5(a)(1) that identifies the physical and environmental
 conditions contained in each zone of an airplane, analyzes the effects of these conditions
 on electrical wiring and components, and assesses the possibilities for smoke and fire.
 The end result of the analysis are inspection and restoration tasks in the form of EWIS
 ICA.
 (b) Electrical Wiring Interconnection System (EWIS): means any wire, power feeder, wiring
 device, or combination of these, including termination devices, installed in any area of the
 airplane for the purpose of transmitting electrical energy, including data and signals,
 between two or more intended termination points. EWIS is defined in full by 14 CFR
 section 25.1701.

 05-00-00

 D6-37569 Sep 25/2016

 (c) The Zonal Inspection Program includes a general visual and, if required, physical check
 of the general condition and security of attachment of the accessible systems and
 structures items contained in defined zones. This includes checks for degradation such
 as chafing of tubing, loose duct supports, damage to wiring and connected EWIS, cable
 and pulley wear, fluid leaks, electrical bonding, general condition of fasteners, inadequate
 drainage, etc., and general corrosion, not covered in the MSG-3 analysis. The zonal
 inspection is not intended as a quality assurance after maintenance check for
 determining proper reassembly of systems, components, structures, or powerplants. The
 zonal program packages a number of General Visual (GV) Inspections into one or more
 zonal inspections. The program includes any GV inspection tasks required to assure
 security of attachment and general condition of any system or structural items within the
 zone.
 (2) Equivalent Tools, Fixtures, Test Equipment, and Consumable Materials
 (a) When the procedures in this manual identify tools, equipment, and consumable materials,
 you can use equivalent alternatives. If you use alternative tools, equipment, or
 consumable materials, make sure that they give the same results and are as safe to the
 parts and personnel as the tools, equipment, or consumable materials specified in the
 procedure.

5. Daily Check Items - Internal Cabin
 A. Passenge Cabin
 SUBTASK 05-00-00-210-001

 (1) Visually check that all emergency exit hatches are secured and that handles are properly
 stowed.

SUBTASK 05-00-00-200-001

 (1) Engine
A. Top off engine oil on both No. 1 and No. 2 engines after 5 minutes from the engine MPD B12-13-11-A
 shut down, but not greater than 60 minutes, then record consumption.
B. Check engine cowling, inlet cowls, nose domes and visible fan blades for obvious MPD C71-11-00-A
 damage. Check access panels and blowout panels for condition and security. Also
 check for open latches and obvious signs of fuel and hydraulic leaks.
 (2) Wheel Wells
A. Check nose and main landing gear tires, wheels and brakes for obvious MPD B32-00-00-E
 damage.
B. Visually check condition of nose & main lading gear viewing windows. Clean MPD B56-41-00-A
 as required.
C. Check the nose and main landing gear tires for the following conditions: MPD B32-45-00-A
 A) Extent and pattern of normal thread wear
 B) Cuts in treads and sidewalls
 C) Cracks or tears in tread
 D) Openings of any splices in tread or side walls
 E) Presence of any bulges or blisters
 F) Indication or chaffing between tire and wheel
 G) Significant spillage of hydraulic fluid onto tire surface

SUBTASK 05-00-00-200-002

 (1) Fuselage
A. Check fuselage access/service panels, cabin windows, hatches, MPD 52-00-00-TR
 navigation/communication antennas and radome from ground level for
 obvious damage and security. Verify that cargo door latches are fully
 engaged. In particular, double check the aft cargo doors on 737-400 models
 LN# 1487-2160, to verify that latches are fully engaged. Masts and drains for
 fluid leakage.

titulo: Corrosion Prevention - Hydraulic System Components in Wheelwell
procedimento:
SUBTASK 05-00-29-211-001

 (1) Examine all exposed hydraulic tubing, valves and fittings in the wheelwell and check for
 corrosion. Pay particular attention to support clamps and surrounding structure (CPM 20-20-00
 Volume 1, CPM 29-10-37 Volume 2) .
 SUBTASK 05-00-29-350-001

 (2) Remove corrosion and rework tubing and components as necessary. Perform touch-up of the
 finish when practical (CPM 29-10-37 Volume 2).
 SUBTASK 05-00-29-390-001

 CAUTION: DO NOT APPLY BMS 3-23 TO SILICONE RUBBER, RUBBER CLAMP CUSHIONS OR
 SKYDROL SEALS. OBSERVE OTHER PRECAUTIONS INDICATED IN VOL. 1,
 SECTION 20-60-00 (PAGES 3 AND 4) OF THE CORROSION PREVENTION MANUAL.
 (3) Apply corrosion inhibiting compound, G00009 with a clean cloth wetted with the corrosion
 inhibiting compound. Avoid excessive application (CPM 29-10-37 Volume 2).
 NOTE: If, at any time the wheelwell is cleaned with high pressure water and detergents or
 steam, reapply corrosion inhibiting compound, G00009.

 rivet heads or white powdery deposits.

 evidence of corrosion (CPM 20-20-00 Volume 1, CPM 57-10-37 Volume 2, Figure 1).
 NOTE: Inspect this area very carefully due to difficulty in corrosion detection caused by the
 dark color and opaqueness of Corogard finishes on current production airplanes.
 Corrosion in this area, which is primary structure, could result in fuel leaks on those
 aircraft equipped with integral center fuel tanks.
 SUBTASK 05-00-53-916-004

 (2) Determine extent of corrosion or other damage to skin finish. Remove corrosion. Restore
 protective finishes to the extent possible. Repair broken finishes by applying BMS 10-79 primer
 and 2 coats of Corogard EC843 coating (CPM 57-30-37 Volume 2, Figure 1).
 SUBTASK 05-00-53-916-005

 CAUTION: PRIOR TO APPLICATION OF BMS 3-23 COMPOUND, OBSERVE PRECAUTIONS
 LISTED IN VOL. 1, SECTION 20-60-00, PAGES 3 AND 4 OF THE CORROSION
 PREVENTION MANUAL.
 (3) Apply corrosion inhibiting compound, G00009 to fastener heads or edges of skin panels,
 especially where paint system has cracked or flaked. Ensure excess compound is wiped off
 (CPM 20-60-00 Volume 1, CPM 57-10-37 Volume 2, Figure 1).

titulo: Corrosion Prevention - Lower Lobe Interior Structure -- Forward
procedimento:
SUBTASK 05-00-53-211-003

 (1) Remove forward cargo compartment floor panels and check bilge areas under forward cargo
 compartment between stringers 25 L and R for corrosion (CPM 53-10-37 Volume 2, Figure 2).
 SUBTASK 05-00-53-902-001

 (2) Remove corrosion, replace broken or damaged finishes and accomplish repairs to fuselage
 structure as necessary (CPM 53-10-37 Volume 2, Figure 1).
 SUBTASK 05-00-53-916-006

 (3) Apply corrosion inhibiting compound, G00009 to all exposed lower lobe structure including
 skin, floor beams, frames, stringers and bulkheads. Pay particular attention to the spraying of

 NOTE: Allow the compound sufficient time to dry on the lower lobe structure before reinstalling
 the insulation blankets. Ensure that the blankets are not wetted with corrosion
 inhibiting compound, G00009 to preclude potential fire hazards.

titulo: Corrosion Prevention - Forward Lower Lobe Interior Structure
procedimento:
NOTE: Corrosion treatment of inner structure may be performed during scheduled
 overhaul/structural inspection of the airplane or at the first opportunity when scheduled work
 allows access to any area of the fuselage. The bilge areas, in particular, should require
 more frequent inspections and application of corrosion inhibiting compound, G00009.
 SUBTASK 05-00-53-211-007

 (1) With panels, forward sidewall lining, and insulation blankets removed, examine the lower
 fuselage interior skin surfaces including frames, stringers, straps, lap splices, shear ties, butt
 joints, faying surfaces and the lower aft face of the fwd (as visible) bulkhead, with emphasis on
 bilge areas (S25L to R) drain paths and overboard drains. Check for broken or deteriorated
 finishes, evidence of corrosion such as skin bulges, loose or missing fasteners and white
 powdery deposits (CPM 20-20-00 Volume 1, CPM 53-10-37 Volume 2, Figure 2, CPM
 53-30-37 Volume 2, Figure 3).
 SUBTASK 05-00-53-350-001

 (2) Remove corrosion, replace broken or damaged finishes and accomplish repair to fuselage
 structure, as necessary (CPM 53-10-37 Volume 2, Figure 1, CPM 53-30-37 Volume 2, Figure
 1).
 SUBTASK 05-00-53-916-011

 (3) Apply corrosion inhibiting compound, G00009 to all exposed lower lobe structure including
 skin, floor beams, frames, stringers, and aft bulkhead. Pay particular attention to the spraying
 of corrosion inhibiting compound, G00009 on lap joints, rivet heads, and stringers below the
 cargo compartment flooring (CPM 20-60-00 Volume 1, CPM 53-10-37 Volume 2, Figure 1 thru
 3).
 NOTE: Allow the compound sufficient time to dry on the lower lobe structure before reinstalling
 the insulation blankets. Ensure that the blankets are not wetted with corrosion
 inhibiting compound, G00009 to preclude potential fire hazards.
 Apply primer, C00259 to inboard flange surfaces of stringers. Replace leveling
 compounds as required.

titulo: Corrosion Prevention - Aft Lower Lobe Interior Structure
procedimento:
NOTE: Corrosion treatment of inner structure may be performed during scheduled
 overhaul/structural inspection of the airplane or at the first opportunity when scheduled work
 allows access to any area of the fuselage. The bilge areas, in particular, should require
 more frequent inspections and application of corrosion inhibiting compound, G00009.
 SUBTASK 05-00-53-211-008

 (1) With panels, aft sidewall lining, and insulation blankets removed, examine the lower fuselage
 interior skin surfaces including frames, stringers, straps, lap splices, shear ties, butt joints,
 faying surfaces, and the aft bulkhead, with emphasis on bilge areas (S25L to R), drain paths
 and overboard drains. Check for broken or deteriorated finishes, evidence of corrosion such as
 skin bulges, loose or missing fasteners and white powdery deposits. In particular, check drain
 hole on station 1016 frame flange for blockage (CPM 20-20-00 Volume 1, CPM 53-10-37
 Volume 2, Figure 2, CPM 53-30-37 Volume 2, Figure 3).
 SUBTASK 05-00-53-350-002

 (2) Remove corrosion, replace broken or damaged finishes and accomplish repair to fuselage
 structure, as necessary (CPM 53-10-37 Volume 2, Figure 1, CPM 53-30-37 Volume 2, Figure
 1).
 SUBTASK 05-00-53-916-012

 (3) Apply corrosion inhibiting compound, G00009 to all exposed lower lobe structure including
 skin, floor beams, frames, stringers, and aft bulkhead. Pay particular attention to the spraying
 of corrosion inhibiting compound, G00009 on lap joints, rivet heads, and stringers below the
 cargo compartment flooring (CPM 20-60-00 Volume 1, CPM 53-10-37 Volume 2, Figure 1 thru
 3).
 NOTE: Allow the compound sufficient time to dry on the lower lobe structure before reinstalling
 the insulation blankets. Ensure that the blankets are not wetted with corrosion
 inhibiting compound, G00009 to preclude potential fire hazards.
 Apply primer, C00259 to inboard flange surfaces of stringers. Replace leveling
 compounds as required.

titulo: Corrosion Prevention - Upper Lobe Interior Structure
procedimento:
NOTE: Corrosion prevention maintenance should be performed at any time access is available to
 the aircraft interior or primarily when the aircraft is scheduled for overhaul/structural
 inspection (CPM 53-10-37 Volume 2, Figure 1).
 SUBTASK 05-00-53-211-009

 (1) With forward interior panels and insulation blankets removed, examine the fuselage crown
 area (S-6L to S-6R) and side panel area (S-6L and 6R to S-17L and 17R) longitudinal lap
 splices, stringers, butt joints and faying surfaces. Specifically check for broken or deteriorated
 finishes and for corrosion as evidenced by skin bulges, loose or missing fasteners and white
 powdery deposits. Also check for doubler-to-skin delamination (CPM 20-20-00 Volume 1, CPM
 53-10-37 Volume 2, Figure 1, CPM 53-30-37 Volume 2, Figure 3).
 SUBTASK 05-00-53-350-003

 (2) Remove corrosion, replace broken or damaged finishes and accomplish repair to fuselage
 structure, as necessary (CPM 57-10-37 Volume 2, Figure 1, CPM 53-30-37 Volume 2, Figure
 1CPM 53-30-37 Volume 2, Figure 1).
 SUBTASK 05-00-53-370-001

 (3) Apply primer, C00259 to inboard flanges stringers (CPM 57-10-37 Volume 2, Figure 1).
 SUBTASK 05-00-53-916-013

 (4) Apply corrosion inhibiting compound, G00009 to all exposed inner fuselage structure. Pay
 particular attention to application of the corrosion inhibitor into lap joints, rivet heads, stringers,
 and faying surfaces (CPM 20-60-00 Volume 1, CPM 53-10-37 Volume 2, Figure 1, CPM
 53-30-37 Volume 2, Figure 3).
 NOTE: Wipe excess compound and allow structure sufficient time to dry before reinstalling the
 insulation blankets. (Ensure the insulation blankets are not wetted with corrosion
 inhibiting compound, G00009 to preclude potential fire hazards.)
 SUBTASK 05-00-53-390-003

 (5) Apply BMS 5-95, Class F sealant to inner flanges of stringers and edges of frames where
 contacted by insulation blankets above the window belt, between BS 259.5 and BS 1015, as
 required.

titulo: Corrosion Prevention - Aft Pressure Bulkhead, Station 1016 - Forward Face
procedimento:
SUBTASK 05-00-53-211-010

 (1) Examine the lower part of the forward face of the pressure bulkhead with special emphasis on
 web lap splices, fastener heads, panel edges, facing surfaces and the lower portion of the
 frame. Check the bulkhead for corrosion and condition of protective finishes. Clean plugged
 drains as required (CPM 20-20-00 Volume 1, CPM 53-10-37 Volume 2, Figure 8).
 NOTE: The drain hole is located on the vertical flange of the bulkhead frame, 7 tenths left of
 bottom centerline. It may be enlarged to 1/2 inch diameter as long as the bottom of the
 enlarged hole remains tangent to the bottom of the existing hole.
 SUBTASK 05-00-53-350-004

 (2) Remove corrosion if any and restore damaged or broken finishes to the extent possible.
 Restore any deteriorated or disbonded leveling compound with adhesive, A01076 material.
 Make sure that sealant does not obstruct the drain hole (CPM 53-10-37 Volume 2, Figure 5).
 SUBTASK 05-00-53-916-014

 PREVENTION MANUAL.
 (3) Apply corrosion inhibiting compound, G00009 to the forward surface of the bulkhead with
 emphasis on fastener heads, panel edges and faying surfaces (CPM 20-60-00 Volume 1, CPM
 53-10-37 Volume 2, Figure 8).

titulo: Corrosion Prevention - Main Deck Floor Structure
procedimento:
NOTE: Corrosion treatment of the galley and lavatory area structure may be performed during
 scheduled overhaul/structural inspection of the airplane or at the first opportunity when
 scheduled work allows access to any area of the fuselage.
 SUBTASK 05-00-53-211-017

 (1) During regularly scheduled structural inspection or overhaul of the airplane when seats,
 carpeting, galleys and lavatories are normally removed, clean and inspect the floor, floor
 structure, all seat/cargo tracks for broken or deteriorated finishes & for evidence of corrosion.
 Inspection should include floor panels, frames, seat track beams and transverse floor beams.
 Also, open plugged drains & clear all drain paths (CPM 20-20-00 Volume 1, CPM 53-10-37
 Volume 2, Figure 3 & 6).
 SUBTASK 05-00-53-350-011

 (2) Remove corrosion and repair or replace broken or damaged finishes, leveling compounds, and
 floor/track sections, as required. Restore the track finish & reapply sealant to flanges & frames
 as necessary (CPM 53-10-37 Volume 2, Figure 1 & 3).

titulo: Corrosion Prevention - Wing Trailing Edge Flaps
procedimento:
SUBTASK 05-00-57-211-008

 (1) Examine the wing trailing edge flaps including skin panels, fasteners, flap tracks and track
 attachment fittings on the rear spar for broken or damaged finishes and evidence of corrosion
 (CPM 20-20-00 Volume 1, CPM 57-50-37 Volume 2, Figure 1).
 SUBTASK 05-00-57-350-008

 (2) Remove corrosion and restore finish to extent possible (CPM 57-50-37 Volume 2, Figure 1).
 SUBTASK 05-00-57-916-006

 CAUTION: PRIOR TO APPLICATION OF BMS 3-23 COMPOUND, OBSERVE PRECAUTIONS
 LISTED IN VOL. 1, SECTION 20-60-00, PAGES 3 AND 4 OF THE CORROSION
 PREVENTION MANUAL.
 (3) Apply corrosion inhibiting compound, G00009 to the flap tracks, track attach fittings, movable
 flap track fairings and flap skin panels having damaged paint finishes (CPM 20-60-00 Volume
 1, CPM 57-50-37 Volume 2, Figure 1).
 NOTE: Do not apply corrosion inhibiting compound, G00009 to silicone rubber or rubber seals.
 Protect all lubricated surfaces and bearings when applying corrosion inhibiting
 compound, G00009.
 NOTE: Whenever cleaning of flaps and flap wells is accomplished with steam or high pressure
 water and detergent, reapply corrosion inhibiting compound, G00009 to the trailing
 edge flaps and components noted in paragraph 1.
 NOTE: After application of corrosion inhibiting compound, G00009, all grease fittings in the
 treated areas should be regreased.

procedimento:
(1) This inspection is used to find if the high strength steel that showed signs of heat damage, had
 changed. It will look for a change in the temper or heat treat properties.
 NOTE: Refer to product Material Safety Data Sheets (MSDS) and local requirements for
 proper handling procedures.

 WARNING: DO NOT BREATHE THE VAPORS OF THE SOLVENTS OR ETCH SOLUTIONS. DO
 NOT GET THEM IN YOUR EYES, ON YOUR SKIN OR ON YOUR CLOTHES. INJURY
 TO PERSONS MAY OCCUR.
 (2) This inspection will usually occur on the components of the landing gear axles. The signs of
 discolored or blistered paint or plating shows that a general intense heat has changed the
 temper of the axle. When this happens, the ammonium persulphate procedure should be
 applied to the damaged part of the axle. Do this procedure after the axles have been reworked.
 Axle rework procedures can be found in Chapter 32, Landing Gear.
SUBTASK 05-51-07-122-041

 WARNING: DO NOT BREATHE THE VAPORS OF THE SOLVENTS OR ETCH SOLUTIONS. DO
 NOT GET THEM IN YOUR EYES, ON YOUR SKIN OR ON YOUR CLOTHES. INJURY
 TO PERSONS MAY OCCUR.
 (1) Strip the cadmium surface with abrasive cloth, B00102 applied by hand. Strip a minimum area
 of 0.5 in. (12.7 mm) through the area that is not to be tested.
 (a) Strip a minimum area of 0.5 in. (12.7 mm) larger than the area that is to be tested.
 SUBTASK 05-51-07-112-033

 (2) Clean the area to be etched, with solvent, B00081.
 SUBTASK 05-51-07-020-001

 (3) Remove the cadmium plating.
 SUBTASK 05-51-07-282-034

 (4) Apply the ammonium persulphate solution, with a cotton wiper, G00034, on the surface to be
 tested for 30 to 60 seconds.

RAM ALL 05-51-07

 D6-37569 Mar 25/2015

 (1) A mercury spill must be considered hazardous, and immediate action must be taken to isolate,
 inspect, and clean the aircraft.
 (2) The corrosive action of mercury is very rapid in pitting and intergranular.
 (3) Mercury amalgamates quickly with aluminum alloys at room temperature if the oxide film on
 the aluminum has been scratched or damaged.
 (a) Once a small area of aluminum has been amalgamated, corrosion and liquid metal
 embrittlement occurs. This process is accelerated by moisture and particularly by salt
 water.
 (4) The amalgamation of stressed aluminum structure may also result in rapid cracking similar to
 stress corrosion cracking.
 (5) Mercury is not consumed in the amalgamation process. As the aluminum oxidizes, it separates
 from the amalgam and the mercury continues to attack fresh aluminum.
 (6) The presence of organic finishes, greases or a thick continuous oxide layer retards the
 amalgamation process.
 (7) When elemental mercury leaks on to an all-metallic structure, severe structural strength
 degradation can occur.
 (a) The rate of the diffusion of the mercury into a metal is related to the type of metal touched
 by the mercury.
 (b) The diffusion is also related to the type of finish protection on the metal.
 (c) When the diffusion has started, it cannot be stopped.
 (d) Structural degradation after a mercury spill is not always visually apparent until a load is
 applied to the structure.
 (8) The inspection, removal, or repair must be made before the next flight.
 (9) Structural repairs are necessary if there are signs of mercury contamination.
 (10) Make sure there is no detectable mercury in the airplane.
 (a) Use mercury sniffers and X-ray equipment (if available) to detect mercury.
 (b) The airplane is only clean when there is no detectable mercury.

(1) This inspection is divided into three phases (Phase I, Phase II and Phase III).
 (a) Phase I (IA and IB) is a general visual inspection for one or more of the following:
 1) The flight crew reported the airplane flight path was through a cloud of visual
 volcanic ash.
 2) The airplane lands or takes off in volcanic ash fallout conditions.
 NOTE: Fallout is identified as ash drifting down from the air, or is blown about by
 the wind. Fallout is also caused by the ash being blown or moved about
 because of the movement of airplanes and ramp vehicles.
 3) An airplane encounters volcanic ash while operating on the ground during volcanic
 ash fallout conditions.
 (b) Phase II is applicable when any of the Phase IB inspections show positive results.
 (c) Phase III is applicable when any of the Phase II inspections show positive results.
 (2) Volcanic ash has the qualities that follow:
 (a) It is hard and highly abrasive.
 (b) It usually contains trace chemicals which can be acidic (pH between 2 and neutral).
 (c) It can cause erosion/abrasion, etching or shot peening on exposed surfaces and remove
 protective finishes.
 (d) The dimensions of most ash particles are less than 5 microns with trace amounts that are
 more than 50 microns.
 (e) It resembles talcum powder.
 (f) It stays on exposed lubricated surfaces.
 (g) Able to enter small orifices and pass by seals.
 (h) Can cause unusual wear and contamination of many airplane systems and filter
 elements.

 WARNING: DO NOT GET VOLCANIC ASH IN YOUR MOUTH, EYES, OR ON YOUR SKIN. PUT
 ON A RESPIRATOR MASK THAT REMOVES VOLCANIC ASH PARTICLES
 SUFFICIENTLY. PUT ON CLOTHES, AND GOGGLES (OR OTHER APPROVED EYE
 PROTECTION) THAT KEEP VOLCANIC ASH OFF YOU. VOLCANIC ASH CAN
 CAUSE INJURIES TO PERSONNEL, AND DAMAGE TO EQUIPMENT.
 (3) Volcanic ash can cause discomfort and injury to persons during fallout conditions, and during
 inspection and cleaning.
 (a) Precautions must be followed when you work in a volcanic ash environment. This will
 prevent the entry of volcanic ash into your eyes and your respiratory (breathing) system.

 (a) Boeing guidance is to always avoid operation in visible ash.

 normal operating and maintenance

procedimento:
(1) This procedure has information for an aircraft that has had an extreme high wind event while
 parked.
 (a) Examples of extreme high wind events are tornadoes and microbursts.
 (b) Examples of evidence of an extreme high wind event are if the airplane moved over the
 chocks or if there are tire skid marks on the ground where the airplane was parked. This
 may indicate that the airplane has moved from the position in which it was originally
 parked.
 1) If the airplane has moved over wheel chocks, it can cause damage to the tires,
 wheels, and landing gear.
 (2) Extreme high wind events are variable and unpredictable.
 (3) Extreme high winds from the side and aft direction while parked can cause damage to the
 aircraft flight control surfaces and flight control mechanisms internal to the wings, horizontal
 stabilizer, and vertical stabilizer. It is possible that this damage will not be seen during a
 walk-around or during pre-flight checks. The integrity of the flight controls is very important to
 the safe flight of the airplane.
 (4) When the conditional inspection tells you to “examine” a component, look for these damage
 conditions:
 • Cracks
 • Twisted parts (distortion)
 • Misalignment
 • Wrinkles
 • Buckles
 • Pulled apart structure
 • Loose paint (paint flakes)
 • Loose fasteners
 • Fasteners that have pulled out or are missing
 • Fastener holes that become larger or longer
 • Delaminations
 • Interference
 • Other signs of damage

 • Cracks

 (1) When persons are in the airplane during this test, they must be in a good physical condition.
 When a person feels pain during a pressure change, you must lower the rate of change of
 pressure, or make the absolute pressure stable immediately. Do this to make sure the person
 can make the pressure equal in their ears. Also, do this to remove the person from the
 airplane.
 (2) This test uses the airplane equipment to pressurize the airplane and monitor the procedure.
 NOTE: A method to calculate absolute pressure is as follows: Determine the field atmospheric
 pressure (in inches of mercury). Divide field atmospheric pressure by 2.036 and add
 the result to the gauge pressure or differential pressure inside the cabin to give the
 absolute pressure (PSIA).
 For example: If the field atmospheric pressure is 29.86 inHG and the cabin differential
 pressure is 4.0 psid, divide 29.86 by 2.036 which equals 14.67 psi. Add the cabin
 differential pressure (in psi) to the field pressure (4.0 psid + 14.67 psi = 18.67 psia) to
 get an absolute pressure of 18.67 psia.
 (a) The primary source to pressurize the airplane is the APU. An optional source to supply air
 to the air conditioning packs is the engine bleed air or an external air source.
 (b) The cabin differential pressure and the rates of pressurization and bleed-down are
 monitored in the control cabin. They are monitored on the differential pressure indicator.
 (3) Many small leakage areas can add to create an excessive fuselage leakage rate. Therefore, it
 is recommended that all sources of leakage be repaired.
 (4) Boeing has determined that all of the following listed equipment may be susceptible to damage
 anytime the cabin pressure exceeds 20 psia. This list is not meant to be all inclusive since

 THE LANDING GEAR EXCEPT FOR THE AXLE JACK PADS AT JACK POINTS F. IF

 FAILURE CAN OCCUR.
 (1) Obey this warning and caution during all of this task.
 (2) There are jack points under each landing gear axle to permit the removal of the wheel and tire
 or brake assembly without the airplane fully lifted.

 between the tires. Use the table for reference only.
 NOTE: The dimensions can change in different conditions.
 (4) Follow these safety instructions when you lift the airplane on jacks:
 (a) Lift only one main gear at a time.
 (b) Remove only one wheel on each gear at a time.

titulo: Balance Check for the Tilted Airplane
procedimento:
(1) When you lift the airplane nose, the center of gravity of the airplane moves aft with respect to
 the main gear axle. This movement, plus the wind, upgrades, and fuel movement can cause
 the airplane to move. This can make the aft fuselage of the airplane touch the ground. Thus,
 you must complete a balance check form to make sure the airplane will be stable. Add the
 ballast, if it is necessary. You can use the dolly as a ballast. To do this, attach it to the nose
 gear wheels.

 (1) Add the moments about the main gear due to these items:
 • Airplane weight (Figure 204)

 • Tow vehicle acceleration (Figure 208)
 • Upgrades (Figure 209)
 SUBTASK 07-13-00-972-023

 (2) Make sure the sum of these moments is more than +1,000,000 inch-pounds.

procedimento:
(1) This procedure has the instructions for the installation of chocks in winds or wind gusts to a

procedimento:
(1) If the complete loss of hydraulic fluid has occurred, do the Hydraulic Fluid Replacement
 procedure (PAGEBLOCK 29-00-00/201).
 (2) If the hydraulic reservoir was filled after the replacement of a component or after fluid loss, do
 the Bleed the Hydraulic System procedure (PAGEBLOCK 29-00-00/201).
 (3) The equipment that is necessary to fill the hydraulic fluid is on the forward bulkhead of the right
 wheel well. The equipment includes a hand pump, a pressure fill connection, a filter for the
 hydraulic fluid, and a selector valve.
 (4) There is a fluid quantity indicator on the system A and B reservoirs. The system B reservoir is
 filled through the standby reservoir. When the fluid quantity indicator for system B shows full,
 the system B reservoir and the standby reservoir are full.
 (5) The fluid chilling at high altitude and the large ambient temperature changes between
 departure and arrival locations can result in a decrease in fluid levels. These cold soak effects
 will not have an impact on the operation of the systems but it can shrink the fluid sufficiently to
 indicate a need for servicing, even if you serviced the reservoirs at a warm location before the
 previous flight. Under such circumstances, if you service the airplane "high" at the cold location
 before the airplane is sent back to the warm location, it is possible that you will cause an
 overfill of the reservoir and fluid can overflow from the drain line.
 (6) If the ambient temperature on the ground is 20°F (-7°C) or lower at an arrival location and a
 fluid level is below "REFILL", service the reservoir to just above "REFILL" to avoid the overflow
 of fluid at the next warmer location.

titulo: Crew Oxygen System Servicing (Cylinder Replacement Method)
procedimento:
(1) Read and obey the safety precautions and the general maintenance instructions of the oxygen
 system before you do the maintenance (PAGEBLOCK 35-00-00/201).
 (2) Oxygen Requirements
 (a) Oxygen that you use in the aircraft oxygen system must have the properties that follow:
 1) The oxygen must contain no less than 99.5% oxygen by volume.
 2) The oxygen must be free from all poisonous contamination to the maximum
 possible level.
 3) The moisture content must not be more than 0.02 milligrams of water vapor for each
 liter of gas at a temperature of 70 degrees Fahrenheit and a pressure of 760
 millimeters of mercury.
 a) Refer to S.A.E. (AS 1065A) for the permitted moisture quantity.
 4) Oxygen of specification MIL-0-27210 of Type 1 agrees with these requirements and
 is recommended.
 (3) Precaution Data
 (a) Make sure that your hands, clothing, tools, area, and equipment are clean and free of
 petroleum materials.
 (b) Keep the oxygen away from ignition sources (heat, sparks and flame) and other material
 that can cause an ignition.
 (c) Keep oxygen away from flammable material, fuel, paint thinners, solvents, and all other
 material that can burn.
 (d) Use only aviation grade oxygen that you can breathe, for the oxygen system.
 (e) Oxygen other than the aviation grade can be satisfactory for you to breathe but it can
 contain too much water.
 (f) Too much water in the oxygen can freeze and can cause clogged lines, regulators, and
 valves of the oxygen system.

titulo: Main Landing Gear Shock Strut Service - Procedure II (Strut dry after repair, or airplane is lifted on
procedimento:
(1) This procedure contains a task to service the shock strut after you drain and disassemble the
 shock strut for repairs or when you add fluid while the airplane is lifted on jacks.
 (2) A procedure to service the shock strut with dry air or nitrogen only is provided in this task.
 CAUTION: DO NOT ADD SMALL QUANTITIES OF HYDRAULIC FLUID WITHOUT LUBRIZOL
 MANY TIMES. IF THERE IS NOT A SUFFICIENT QUANTITY OF LUBRIZOL IN THE
 FLUID, DAMAGE TO THE SHOCK STRUT CAN OCCUR.
 (3) You can add lubricant to the shock strut when servicing. As an alternate method, a fully
 formulated fluid with a lubricant premixed is available. For regular servicing where relatively
 small amounts of fluid is necessary, it is acceptable to use hydraulic oil without added lubricant
 to fill the shock struts.
 (4) Shock Strut Fluids - General
 (a) All of the fluids that are listed here are compatible. Use any of these fluids to top off the
 strut even if the strut was originally filled with one of the other fluids.
 (b) Lubrizol 1395 and methyl oleate are heavy duty lubricants. They are added to the fluid to
 reduce the wear on the parts of the shock strut that move.
 (c) Use BMS 3-32, Type I to fill the shock strut for the first time when new, or after overhaul.
 There is a corrosion inhibitor in the MIL-H-6083 fluid.
 (d) Use BMS 3-32, Type I or Type II at the operator's discretion, for subsequent refills or to
 top off the strut. These two types of fluid are compatible.
 (e) If the proper mixture is not available, You can use MIL-H-6083 or MIL-H-5606 fluid
 without additives to top off the strut.
 Try not to do this, however, because the additive that is already in the strut will become
 more diluted. This will make it less effective.
 (f) It is not necessary to change the seals in the shock strut if you drained the strut and filled
 with one of the other fluids.
 (g) Use the premixed fluid, BMS 3-32 Types I and II, if it is possible. This is more convenient
 for the operator and will remove the possibility of error that can occur when the operator
 mixes the fluids.
 (h) Qualified vendors and vendor codes for the shock strut fluids are listed in
 PAGEBLOCK 20-30-21/201.
 (5) Preferred (Pre-mixed) Shock Strut Fluids
 (a) BMS 3-32, Type I - This is MIL-H-6083 fluid pre-mixed with 1.5 percent by volume of
 Lubrizol 1395 and 1 percent by volume of methyl oleate.
 (b) BMS 3-32, Type II - This is MIL-H-5606 fluid pre-mixed with 1.5 percent by volume of
 Lubrizol 1395 and 1 percent by vol

 about where to lubricate is given in the subsequent subjects of this section.

 equipment removal and replacement.
 (2) General-Purpose Aviation Grease
 (a) Boeing chooses the grease to use based on the specific application. Greases that meet
 the following specifications are considered general-purpose aviation grease for
 applications that operate in the -100°F (-73°C) to 250°F (121°C) range:
 1) BMS 3-33
 2) MIL-PRF-23827
 3) MIL-G-21164 (NATO G-353)
 (b) BMS 3-33 is the preferred general-purpose aviation grease recommended by Boeing for
 applications exposed to temperatures of less than 250°F (121°C). It is recommended
 because it shows better wear, corrosion protection, and low temperature torque
 properties.
 1) BMS 3-33 is satisfactory to be used:
 a) When MIL-PRF-23827 was specified.
 b) When MIL-G-21164 was specified and MIL-PRF-23827 is given as an option.
 c) As a direct replacement for BMS 3-24.
 2) BMS 3-33 cannot be used where MIL-G-21164 or Royco 11MS are the only greases
 specified because BMS 3-33 was found not to be satisfactory in heavily loaded
 sliding applications.
 3) Greases that have been used before and approved by Boeing for the specific
 assembly are listed as flagnotes on the lubrication instructions for the specific
 assembly. If there is an application where only one grease must be used, it will be
 listed with the word "Only" after it.
 (3) Special Performance Greases

titulo: Changing of Approved Grease Brands or Specification Types
procedimento:
(1) Boeing and grease manufacturers agree it is a best practice to limit intermixing of different
 types or brand-names of grease.
 (2) If you mix two different types or brand-names of greases, the performance and properties of
 the mixture may be degraded when compared with the performance and properties of the
 original, unmixed greases.
 (3) Use a different grease (alternative, optional, or brand-name) only after you remove the used
 grease as discussed below either by pumping or disassembly.
 (4) Purging

RAM ALL 12-20-00

 D6-37569 Sep 25/2015

 (a) Purging is the industry-recognized practice of replacing one grease with another. It is also
 the recommended procedure to be following in all lubrication tasks, even when not
 switching from one grease brand or type to another. It is used to ensure that as much of
 the used grease as possible or practical is removed from the assembly and is replaced
 by new grease.
 1) Purge the grease only when it is not possible or practical to disassemble to remove
 the used grease.
 2) The new grease can be the same type or a different type of grease if permitted for
 the application.
 3) Purging removes the contamination (wear debris, etc.) along with the used grease.
 (b) Purging applies both to greasing with a new brand of grease and to usual greasing with
 the same grease.
 (c) When an assembly is purged with a new brand of grease, a quantity of the previously
 used grease can continue to be in the assembly. The subsequent purging from the
 second and third lubrication operations with the new grease will decrease the remaining
 concentration of the previously used grease.
SUBTASK 12-20-00-913-005

 (1) Make sure that the grease that you use is permitted by the specific AMM instructions and your
 local maintenance practices.
 SUBTASK 12-20-00-913-006

 (2) Where surfaces are exposed or disassembly is a practical part of the lubrication procedure
 (e.g., wheel bearings), do these steps to replace the used grease:
 (a) Remove all of the used grease from the bearing surfaces, and internal spaces of the
 mechanism with wipes.
 (b) Lubricate the bearing surfaces with the new grease.
 SUBTASK 12-20-00-913-007

 (3) Where it is not possible or practical to disassemble the mechanism, do these steps to purge
 the used grease:
 (a) Slowly put the new grease into each grease fitting.
 (b) Continue to add grease until all used grease is visually removed and only the new grease
 comes out.

 Reference Title

 SUBTASK 12-22-81-023-011

 (1) Remove the flexible cable from the cable sleeve (PAGEBLOCK 27-62-51/401).
 SUBTASK 12-22-81-643-012

 (2) Lubricate the cable:
 (a) Apply a large quantity of grease to the full length of the cable.
 (b) Apply grease to the surfaces of the swivel tubes and the guide tubes.
 SUBTASK 12-22-81-423-013

 (3) Install the flexible cable (PAGEBLOCK 27-62-51/401).
 SUBTASK 12-22-81-713-014

 (4) Make sure the cable moves freely in the sleeve:
 (a) Make sure the bolt that attaches the lower rod end is not installed.
 (b) Move the cable through its full travel a minimum of six times.
 (c) Make sure the force necessary to push the cable is less than 18.0 pounds.
 (d) Make sure the force necessary to extend the cable is less than 15.0 pounds.
 (e) If the cable does not move in these limits, replace the cable.
 SUBTASK 12-22-81-163-015

 (5) Remove the unwanted grease from the top end of the cable.
 NOTE: Keep a large quantity of grease on all parts in the boot.
 SUBTASK 12-22-81-413-016

 (6) Install the protective boot on the lower end of the cable.
 SUBTASK 12-22-81-433-017

 (7) Install the bolt that attaches the lower rod end.
 SUBTASK 12-22-81-823-018

 (8) Do the adjustment and test of the cable (PAGEBLOCK 27-62-51/501).

 CAUTION: DO NOT USE SOLVENT OR HEAT TO THIN GREASE. DO NOT USE SOLVENT TO
 CLEAN CABLES, SINCE SOLVENT DILUTES AND REMOVES GREASE FROM
 INSIDE CABLE STRANDS. DO NOT APPLY OR SPRAY BMS 3-23 ON CONTROL
 CABLES.
 (1) Use a lint-free cloth, G01043 that is clean and dry to clean the control cables.
 NOTE: Remove the old grease and dirt from the surface of the control cable. Clean the control
 cable for the full length of the cable for the full length of travel through fairleads, air
 pressure seals, over pulleys, quadrants, and drums.
 NOTE: The control cable must be displaced full travel in each direction for complete inspection
 at fairleads, air pressure seals, grommets, quadrants, drums, and over pulleys.
 SUBTASK 12-26-00-643-003

 (2) Lubricate the control cables:
 (a) Carbon Steel Cables:
 NOTE: THE CONTROL CABLES IN THE WING AND NACELLE AREA ARE NEAR
 HIGHTEMPERATURE SOURCES. DETERIORATION OF LUBRICANTS WILL
 OCCUR AT A FASTER RATE THAN ON OTHER CONTROL CABLES.
 1) Apply a light even coat of BMS3-33 grease, D00633 (preferred) or BMS3-24
 grease, D00015 (alternate) to the cable for the full length of travel.
 2) Do not apply grease to these areas because they will receive grease during cable
 movement:
 a) Through the fairleads.
 b) Through the air pressure seals.
 c) On the pulleys.
 d) On the quadrants.
 e) On the drums.
 3) After application of grease on the cable, the cable should be wiped with a clean
 cloth to remove grease, but leave a thin visible film.

titulo: Cold Weather Attended Parking at Temperatures Below 32°F (0°C)

referencias.titulo: MAIN LANDING GEAR SHOCK STRUT - SERVICING
NOSE LANDING GEAR SHOCK STRUT - SERVICING

procedimento:
(1) This task is to park the airplane during cold weather in an attended parking condition. Attended
 parking is generally used when the airplane will be on the ground for a period of time between
 flights and ready for immediate operation.
 (2) During attended parking, the temperature of the cabin and flight deck are maintained warmer
 than 32°F (0°C) and the engines are maintained warmer than -40°F (-40°C) while the airplane
 is on the ground.

 12-33-02

 D6-37569 Sep 25/2015

 (3) For airplanes that operate continuously in cold weather, put the airplane into a heated hangar
 periodically to thaw the insulation blankets and other equipment.
 (4) If the temperature of the fuel is below 32°F (0°C), do not to drain the fuel tank sumps. To check
 for water at the fuel tank sump drain valves with fuel temperature below 32°F (0°C), do this
 task to raise the temperature of the fuel: Fuel Sump Drainage, TASK 12-11-01-683-103-001.
 (5) When adding fuel, you must use these requirements:
 (a) Make sure the fuel temperature is at least 6°F or 3°C above the fuel freeze point. Use the
 ASTM method to determine the freeze point.
 NOTE: The Fuel Quantity Indicator on the wing fuel station can indicate slowly or not
 show numbers in cold conditions. Use an external fuel flow meter to show the
 amount of fuel added to the airplane.
 (b) Use fuels that meet specification ASTM D1655; or
 (c) Use fuels that meet specification GOST 10227:
 1) RT (PT, Russian spelling)
 2) TS-1 (TC-1, Russian spelling)
 (d) Approved fuel additives are:
 NOTE: Adding an anti-icing fuel additive may help in the sumping of the fuel tanks.
 1) Fuel Additive, specification GOST 8313, Fluid I (also known as Fluid E)
 a) Fluid I may be used at a mixture of no more than 0.15 percent by volume.
 2) Fuel Additive, specification TU-6-10-1458, Fluid I-M (also known as Fluid E-
 Methanol).
 NOTE: This fuel additive is not approved for GE engines.
 a) Fluid I-M may be used at a mixture of no more than 0.15 percent each, by
 volume.
 3) Fuel Additive, specification GOST 17477, Fluid TGF.
 NOTE: This fuel additive is not approved for GE engines.
 a) Fluid TGF may be used at a mixture of no more than 0.15 percent by volume.
 4) Fuel Additive, specification TU-6-10-1457, Fluid TGF-M (also known as Fluid TGF-
 Methanol).
 NOTE: This fuel additive is not approved for GE engines.
 a) Fluid TGF-M may be used at a mixture of no more than 0.15 percent each, by
 volume.
 5) Fuel additive, specification ASTM D4171.

titulo: Cold Weather Unattended Parking at Temperatures Below 32F (0C)
procedimento:
(1) This task is to park the airplane during cold weather in an unattended parking condition.
 Unattended parking is generally used when the airplane will be on the ground in a
 non-operational condition between flights.
 (2) During unattended parking, the temperatures of the cabin and flight deck are not maintained
 warmer than 32°F (0°C) and the engines are not maintained warmer than -40°F (-40°C) while
 the airplane is on the ground.
 (3) For airplanes that operate continuously in cold weather, put the airplane into a heated hangar
 periodically to thaw the insulation blankets and other equipment.
 (4) If the temperature of the fuel is below 32°F (0°C), do not to drain the fuel tank sumps. To check
 for water at the fuel tank sump drain valves with fuel temperature below 32°F (0°C), do this
 task to raise the temperature of the fuel: Fuel Sump Drainage, TASK 12-11-01-683-103-001.
 (5) When adding fuel, you must use these requirements:
 (a) Make sure the fuel temperature is at least 6°F or 3°C above the fuel freeze point. Use the
 ASTM method to determine the freeze point.
 NOTE: The Fuel Quantity Indicator on the wing fuel station can indicate slowly or not
 show numbers in cold conditions. Use an external fuel flow meter to show the
 amount of fuel added to the airplane.
 (b) Use fuels that meet specification ASTM D1655; or
 (c) Use fuels that meet specification GOST 10277:
 1) RT (PT, Russian spelling)
 2) TS-1 (TC-1, Russian spelling)
 (d) Approved fuel additives are:
 NOTE: Adding an anti-icing fuel additive may help in the sumping of the fuel tanks.
 1) Fuel Additive, specification GOST 8313, Fluid I (also known as Fluid E)
 a) Fluid I may be used at a mixture of no more than 0.15 percent by volume.
 2) Fuel Additive, specification TU-6-10-1458, Fluid I-M (also known as Fluid E-
 Methanol).
 NOTE: This fuel additive is not approved for GE engines.
 a) Fluid I-M may be used at a mixture of no more than 0.15 percent each, by
 volume.
 3) Fuel Additive, specification GOST 17477, Fluid TGF.
 NOTE: This fuel additive is not approved for GE engines.
 a) Fluid TGF may be used at a mixture of no more than 0.15 percent by volume.
 4) Fuel Additive, specification TU-6-10-1457, Fluid TGF-M (also known as Fluid TGF-
 Methanol).
 NOTE: This fuel additive is not approved for GE engines.
 a) Fluid TGF-M may be used at a mixture of no more than 0.15 percent each, by
 volume.
 5) Fuel additive, specification ASTM D4171.

titulo: Clean the Acoustic Surfaces of the Thrust Reverser
procedimento:
(1) Special attention should be given to prevent water and cleaning agents from entering the
 honeycomb cells of the acoustic panels.
 Follow the steps below to minimize the ingestion of cleaning solutions and water into the
 acoustic panels.

 CAUTION: WATER AND CLEANING AGENTS TRAPPED INSIDE THE PANEL WILL LEAD
 TO CORROSION OF THE ALUMINUM HONEYCOMB CORE.
 (a) Wipe cleaning solutions on with a clean cloth, damp, but not saturated, with cleaning
 solution.
 (b) Wipe with a clean cloth, damp with water, to remove all residues.
 (c) Wipe using a clean dry cloth to remove all moisture.
 (2) Use ONLY cleaning agents certified to the requirements of Document D6-17487, Evaluation of
 Airplane Maintenance Materials, when cleaning acoustic panels.
 CAUTION: DO NOT SUBJECT AREAS CONTAINING PERFORATED SKINS TO HIGH
 PRESSURE SPRAYING, OR SUBMERGE IN SOLVENTS OR WATER.
 (3) If pressure washing is required for components around acoustic panels, the acoustic portion of
 the nacelle should be covered to prevent ingestion of the cleaning solutions.
 (4) Do not vapor degrease Graphite/Aramid epoxy structures with chlorinated cleaning agents
 such as Methylene Chloride, Trichloroethylene, and Trichloroethane. Chlorinated cleaning
 agents will cause damage to Graphite/Aramid epoxy structures.

titulo: Use of Heat Guns, Soldering Guns, and Soldering Irons
procedimento:
(1) This procedure gives the minimum recommended safety procedures for heat guns, soldering
 guns, and soldering irons used near airplanes.
 These are general procedures. If regulations made by local agencies or procedures made by
 the airline are more applicable, use them.
 Boeing cannot know or write about all possible conditions which the airlines can have.
 (2) You must examine the conditions and be careful. Customer airlines must know how heat guns,
 soldering guns, and soldering irons are used.
 (3) Heat guns, soldering guns, and soldering irons can cause an explosion. Components in all of
 these devices can operate at temperatures higher than the fuel ignition temperature (450°F).
 Heat guns and soldering guns also can contain electrical switches which can cause sparks.
 These sparks can cause the fuel to burn.
 (4) We do not recommend you use a device to supply heat in the fuel tanks. You can have a good
 flow of air in the fuel tanks. You can make them safe when you fill the fuel tanks with nitrogen.
 For the repair of the wires in the fuel tanks, we recommend you use procedures that use
 crimped splices and sleeves with nylon ties.
 These procedures are specified in WDM Chapter 20.
 (5) Do not use heat guns, soldering guns, or soldering irons less than 100 feet from an airplane
 during these operations:
 • When you fuel
 • When you defuel
 • When the fuel tanks are open.
 (6) You can use heat guns, soldering guns, and soldering irons when and where smoking is
 permitted. If you use these devices where smoking is not permitted, you must first make sure
 there are not dangerous levels of fuel fumes in the work area.
 (7) Zero is the safe fuel fume level at which to use devices that can cause ignition.
 (8) Monitor the fuel tank environment with a combustible gas indicator that measures these
 conditions:
 • Oxygen Concentration
 • Lower Explosive Limit (LEL)
 • Parts per Million (PPM) of Combustible Gas
 (9) You can use the Gastech GT-Series combustible gas indicator to monitor the fuel tank
 environment. If an alarm goes off, one of several conditions has occurred:
 • A liquid fuel or fume source is near
 • The oxygen content is too low
 • The long term fuel exposure limit is above the health limits
 • The local fuel fume levels are high or the ventilation is not sufficient.

(1) Software Installation Times
 (a) The time required to install software in a component is variable and is dependent on
 several factors that include:
 1) Retrieval of the correct software media, applicable equipment and Maintenance
 Manual procedure.
 2) Setup procedures.
 3) Data transfer time.
 4) Software configuration check.
 5) Return to usual airplane configuration.
 6) Airline completion procedures.
 (2) Data Transfer Times
 (a) The data transfer time is the actual time from disk or disks insertion into the data loader
 until the data transfer is complete.
 (b) The data transfer time depends on:
 1) The number of disks.
 2) The type and size of software files on each disk.
 3) The unique protocols and processors of the data loader.
 4) The unique internal protocols and processors of the component.
 5) Disks inserted in a timely manner.
 (c) Typical data transfer times are:
 1) Operational Program Software (OPS): approximately 5 to 16 minutes per disk; for
 example, if the OPS has four disks, then the complete installation can take as long
 as 64 minutes.
 2) Operational Program Configuration (OPC): approximately 1 to 3 minutes per disk.
 3) Databases: approximately 3 to 15 minutes per disk.

4. Measure Airplane Electrical Resistance to Ground
 NOTE: This procedure is a scheduled maintenance task.

 (1) Ohmmeter - Multimeter
 B. References
 Reference Title

 POWER)
 C. Tools/Equipment
 NOTE: When more than one tool part number is listed under the same "Reference" number, the
 tools shown are alternates to each other within the same airplane series. Tool part numbers
 that are replaced or non-procurable are preceded by "Opt:", which stands for Optional.

RAM ALL 20-40-11

 D6-37569 Mar 25/2015

 Reference Description
 COM-6457 Meter - Insulation (Range: 1-1,000 VDC or equivalent, select meter
 per test requirements)
 737-400HGW, -500
 Part #: 1863-9700 Supplier: 62015

 Opt Part #: 1865-00-CE Supplier: 62015
 D. Prepare to Check
 SUBTASK 20-40-11-042-008

 (1) Remove electrical power from the airplane (PAGEBLOCK 24-22-00/201).
 SUBTASK 20-40-11-042-014

 (2) Remove or De-energize any External Powered devices.
 SUBTASK 20-40-11-762-018

 (3) Do a continuity check from the neutral pin of the external power receptacle to the grounding
 stud.
 (a) Make sure the resistance does not exceed 0.1 ohms.
 SUBTASK 20-40-11-042-015

 (4) Disconnect airplane static ground cables if connected.
 SUBTASK 20-40-11-422-009

 (5) Connect a insulation meter, COM-6457 between the recognized bonding/grounding point in the
 wheel well area and an identified ground point on the ramp or the surface of the ramp on which
 the airplane is parked.
 SUBTASK 20-40-11-420-001

 (6) Set the megohmmeter to the 50 Vdc range.
 SUBTASK 20-40-11-762-010

 (7) Measure the resistance to ground and record in the maintenance log. Resistance should be
 less than 1.0 megohms.
 SUBTASK 20-40-11-282-019

 (8) If the resistance exceeds 1.0 megohms this may be the result of inadequate grounding point or
 exceptional high surface resistance.

procedimento:
(1) This procedure is for on-the-ground maintenance.
 (a) Circuit breakers open when there is an electrical overload in the airplane system. A circuit
 breaker that opens because of an electrical overload is known as a "tripped" circuit
 breaker.
 (b) You must use the ENGINE FUEL FEED SYSTEM - TROUBLE SHOOTING,
 PAGEBLOCK 28-22-00/101 for troubleshooting open (tripped) fuel pump circuit breakers.
 1) You can not use this procedure to reset a tripped fuel pump circuit breaker.
 NOTE: Reset of the fuel pump circuit breakers is a Critical Design Configuration
 Control Limitation (CDCCL) item.
 (c) If there are currently specific instructions for the reset of a tripped circuit breaker in
 maintenance and troubleshooting procedures, follow those instructions.
 (d) A defective circuit breaker can cause the circuit breaker to open. Make sure that the
 circuit breaker is serviceable.
 (e) Use your judgement and airline policy to reset a tripped circuit breaker.
 (f) Monitor the airplane to see if a tripped circuit breaker occurs again on subsequent flights.
 (g) Do not reset a tripped circuit breaker until you know the cause for the tripped circuit
 breaker and that the circuit breaker can be safely reset. Fires have occurred in which the
 tripped circuit breakers were reset without an examination of the cause.
 (h) Use this procedure to reset a tripped circuit breaker:
 1) If you know that the circuit breaker is serviceable.
 2) If this procedure is in agreement with your airline policy.
 3) If you cannot determine the cause for the tripped circuit breaker.
 4) If you cannot determine whether it is safe to reset the circuit breaker.
SUBTASK 20-60-01-862-002

 (1) Attach a DO-NOT-CLOSE tag to the tripped circuit breaker.
 SUBTASK 20-60-01-862-003

 (2) Install a circuit breaker lock on the tripped circuit breaker.
 SUBTASK 20-60-01-862-004

 (3) If the tripped circuit breaker is one of three circuit breakers protecting a 3-phase circuit:

 (b) Attach DO-NOT-CLOSE tags.

 (a) The condition existing when the circuit breaker trip occurred.

 (c) The results of resetting the circuit breaker.

procedimento:
(1) This procedure is an enhanced zonal analysis procedure (EZAP) task.
 (2) This procedure cleans the area(s) and/or items(s) to significantly reduce the accumulation of
 combustible material.
 B. Definition:
 (1) A combustible material is any solid, liquid, or gaseous material that has the ability to cause a
 fire to be sustained after removal of the ignition source. Refer to Advisory Circular AC 25-27 for
 additional information regarding combustible materials and wiring contamination.
SUBTASK 20-60-02-010-001

 (1) Do this task: Static Ground Procedure, TASK 20-40-11-862-001.

 WARNING: EXERCISE EXTREME CAUTION WHEN WORKING AROUND ENERGIZED PANELS.
 HIGH VOLTAGES PRESENT CAN BE FATAL.
 (2) If it is necessary to touch the EWIS, it is recommended to remove electrical power in the
 area(s) or from the item(s) to be cleaned:
 NOTE: You can remove all electrical power from the airplane if the removal from one or more
 systems is not possible.
 (a) Identify the applicable electrical system(s) in the area(s) and/or from the item(s) to be
 cleaned.
 (b) Open circuit breakers and switches for the applicable area(s) and/or from the item(s) to
 be cleaned.
 (c) Put a collar/warning tag on the applicable circuit breaker(s), and warning tag on the
 applicable switch(s) for the area(s) and/or from the item(s) to be cleaned.
 (3) Remove panels as necessary to gain access to the area(s)/item(s).

 20-60-02

 D6-37569 Mar 25/2015

 SUBTASK 20-60-02-160-001

 (4) Do these steps to clean the area(s)/item(s):
 NOTE: This procedure cleans the area(s)/item(s) where significant combustible material
 accumulates.
 (a) Do this task: Protection of the EWIS During Maintenance, TASK 20-60-07-913-801.

 CAUTION: DO NOT CUT, CAUSE NICKS, OR CAUSE OTHER DAMAGE TO THE CABLES,
 WIRES, METAL-BRAIDED SHIELD, OR OVERBRAID. DAMAGE TO THESE
 COMPONENTS CAN CAUSE MALFUNCTIONS, OR DAMAGE TO OTHER
 EQUIPMENT.
 (b) Remove loose contamination by hand.
 (c) Use a vacuum, STD-10711 with a soft bristle brush head to remove accumulations of

(1) This procedure is for on-the-ground maintenance and is preventative maintenance for those
 circuit breakers that are less frequently used. It is not necessary to do this procedure for
 frequently used circuit breakers. Because each airline operates differently, it is an airline
 decision as to which circuit breakers are frequently used and which circuit breakers are less
 frequently used.
 (2) Research has shown that the cycling of less frequently used circuit breakers can help to
 improve operational system reliability. If a circuit breaker has not been operated for some time,
 it is possible that the circuit breaker may not open when an electrical fault occurs.
 (3) Circuit breakers are located in all areas of the airplane such as the flight compartment,
 electrical equipment bays, cargo compartments, passenger compartment, and other areas.
 (4) Too much repeated use of a circuit breaker can result in premature failure of the circuit breaker.

titulo: Protection of the EWIS During Maintenance
procedimento:
(1) Definition:
 (a) Electrical Wiring Interconnection System (EWIS): means any wire, power feeder, wiring
 device, or combination of these, including termination devices, installed in any area of the
 airplane for the purpose of transmitting electrical energy, including data and signals,
 between two or more intended termination points. EWIS is defined in full by 14 CFR
 section 25.1701.
 (2) This procedure gives instructions for the installation of temporary protection for EWIS during
 maintenance work when contamination or mechanical damage can occur.
 (3) Protect all airplane EWIS, regardless of the gauge or insulation material, during airplane
 maintenance to prevent or significantly decrease the potential for damage from contamination
 and debris.
 (a) Protection of EWIS starts with identification of the potential for contamination or
 mechanical damage.
 (b) The protection ends with making sure that EWIS is free of all sources of contamination.
 (c) Prevention and frequent removal of contamination during all maintenance work is
 necessary to maintain EWIS in an airworthy condition.
 (d) EWIS can be easily damaged during removal of airplane equipment, or if it is used as a
 handhold or support for personal equipment.
 (e) In general, EWIS that is undisturbed and kept free of contamination will provide
 trouble-free service without the need for unscheduled maintenance.
 (4) To maintain necessary properties of EWIS, it must be kept free of chemicals and debris.
 (a) Hydraulic fluid is a common cause of wire bundle and wire component degradation.
 Hydraulic fluid is very damaging to connector grommets, wire bundle clamps, and to wire
 insulation when exposed over a long time. This can cause indirect damage such as
 arcing and chafing, and break down of the insulation.
 (5) Make sure that EWIS is protected from the accumulation of contamination before you start
 maintenance work such as servicing, repairing, cleaning, or modifying.

 than 3 inches long.
 (3) This task includes steps to install insulation material on the air duct.
 (4) CFR 14 Part 121.312 mandates that insulation material installed in the fuselage as a

 (7) Air conditioning ducts with polyimide foam insulation, G02470 must be wrapped with tape,
 G50327 to meet the flammability/flame propagation requirements. Wrap the tape, G50327
 across 100% of the brown hypalon insulation surface on the polyimide foam insulation,
 G02470.
 (8) Do not use BMS8-39 polyurethane foam insulation for repairs due to the degradation in
 flammability properties over time.

titulo: Structural Repair - Fiberglass or Kevlar Duct
procedimento:
(1) This procedure gives instructions for making a structural repair to a fiberglass or Kevlar air
 conditioning duct.
 (2) A structural repair is applicable when the damage to the air conditioning duct is a cut or a hole
 that is more than 1/4 inch wide and more than 3 inches long but less than 5 percent of the total
 surface area of the duct. If the damage is more than 5 percent of the total surface area of the
 duct, replace the duct section.
 (3) This task includes steps to install insulation material on the air duct.

 flammability properties over time.

 across 100% of the brown hypalon insulation surface of the polyimide foam.

titulo: Insulation Replacement - Air Conditioning Distribution Duct with AN-26 Insulation Blankets
procedimento:
(1) This procedure provides instruction for the replacement of AN-26 insulation on specified ducts.
 Service Bulletins 25-1554 and 25-1572 note the airplane effectivities and air conditioning ducts
 applicable to this procedure. This procedure may also be applicable to insulation on ducts
 installed in the flight deck.
 (2) This replacement will be necessary if the duct is replaced or the insulation is damaged.
 (3) These AN-26 insulation blankets are strengthened with a tough, transparent coating of
 polyethylene terephthalate (PET) whose fire resistant properties decrease with time and
 contamination. If the insulation on a duct is replaced with the AN-26 blanket, the fire resistant
 properties of the insulation needs to be increased with application of a fire retardant treatment
 to meet the more stringent flame propagation standards specified in CFR Part 25.856, effective
 September 2, 2003.
 (4) The procedures in this task may also apply to air conditioning ducts with AN-26 insulation in
 the control cabin conditioned air distribution system (PAGEBLOCK 21-22-00/001 ).

SUBTASK 21-32-11-014-002

 (1) Remove the aft bulkhead panel (right) in the aft cargo compartment to get access to the
 pressure and relief valve.
 SUBTASK 21-32-11-024-011

 (2) Remove the relief valve door from the frame:
 (a) Remove the valve hinge bolts.
 (b) Disengage the spring from the frame anchor hole.
 NOTE: Do not permit the spring to move suddenly out of the frame anchor hole. Hold the
 spring while you lower it against the relief valve door.
 (c) Remove the relief valve door.
 SUBTASK 21-32-11-034-012

 (3) Remove the spring from the relief valve door:
 (a) Remove the fasteners which hold the spring support retainer to the relief valve door and
 remove the retainer.
 (b) Hold the spring while you remove the spring support rod.
 (c) Disengage the spring from the anchor hole in the relief valve door.
 NOTE: The spring will turn approximately 360°.

SUBTASK 21-32-11-434-013

 (1) Install the spring to the relief valve door:
 (a) Put the spring on the spring support rod.
 (b) Put the spring tang through the small hole in the door lug.
 (c) Put the end of the sring support rod through the large hole in the door lug.
 (d) Turn the spring approximately 360° and hold it in that position.
 (e) Put the free end of the spring support rod in the slot on the other door lug.
 (f) Put the free end of the spring against the edge of the relief valve door.
 (g) Put the spring support retainer in its position and install the fasteners.
 SUBTASK 21-32-11-214-014

 (2) Examine the condition of the seal in the frame and replace it if it is damaged.
 SUBTASK 21-32-11-424-015

 (3) Install the relief valve door to the frame:
 (a) Put the relief valve door in the frame.
 (b) Put the free end of the spring through the frame anchor hole.
 (c) Apply the grease, D00013 (PAGEBLOCK 20-30-21/201) to the valve hinge bolts.
 (d) Install the valve hinge bolts.
 (e) Remove the unwanted grease, D00013 if it is necessary.

titulo: Test Safety Relief Valve Using Hamilton Standard Test Fixture
procedimento:
SUBTASK 21-32-21-845-002

 (1) Prepare for the test:
 (a) Close the pressure regulator on the pressure relief valve tester, SPL-6692.
 (b) Connect the air source to the pressure regulator on the pressure relief valve tester,
 SPL-6692.
 SUBTASK 21-32-21-725-003

 (2) Do the test:

 WARNING: MANUALLY HOLD THE VACUUM HEAD ASSEMBLY AGAINST THE AIRPLANE
 FUSELAGE DURING THE TEST. IF YOU DO NOT MANUALLY HOLD THE
 VACUUM HEAD ASSEMBLY, IT CAN FALL FROM THE FUSELAGE SURFACE
 DURING THE TEST. INJURY TO PERSONNEL OR DAMAGE TO EQUIPMENT
 CAN OCCUR.
 (a) Put the pressure relief valve tester, SPL-6692 on the safety relief valve on the fuselage.

 21-32-21

 D6-37569 Sep 25/2015

 (b) Put the locating crossbar on the pressure relief valve tester, SPL-6692 forward of the
 deflector tube on the safety relief valve and hold the pressure relief valve tester,
 SPL-6692 in position.
 NOTE: The fixture is installed to make sure that the test fixture gasket is not on the
 opening in the valve.
 (c) Open the air pressure regulator on the pressure relief valve tester, SPL-6692 to start the
 flow of air.
 (d) Adjust the air pressure regulator so that the indication on the vacuum gage increases 4.5
 inch Hg/minute until the vacuum gage shows 15.8 inch Hg.
 (e) When the vacuum gage shows 15.8 inch Hg, adjust the air pressure regulator to increase
 the vacuum in 0.1 inch Hg increments.
 (f) Stop the increase of vacuum for 10 seconds between each increase of 0.1 inch Hg.
 (g) Continue the intermittent vacuum increases of 0.1 inch Hg until the valve opens.
 (h) Monitor the indication on the vacuum gage when the valve opens.
 (i) Make sure the valve opens between 8.01 to 8.35 psi (16.3 to 17.0 inches of Hg).
 (j) Close the pressure regulator on the valve test fixture.
 (k) Remove the valve test fixture from the airplane.
 (l) Disconnect the air source from the pressure regulator.
 SUBTASK 21-32-21-725-008

 (3) Do the test for the other safety relief valve.

titulo: Test Safety Relief Valve Using Boeing Test Equipment
procedimento:
SUBTASK 21-32-21-845-005

 (1) Prepare for the test:
 (a) Make sure all the valves on the pressure relief valve tester, SPL-6692 are closed.
 (b) Connect the the air pressure source to the quick-disconnect air connection on the
 pressure relief valve tester, SPL-6692.
 (c) Make sure the vacuum regulator valve on the pressure relief valve tester, SPL-6692 is
 turned fully clockwise.
 (d) Adjust the air control valve until the indication on the pressure gage is 70 (+10/-10) psi.
 (e) Adjust the vacuum regulator valve until the differential pressure is approximately 2.0 psi.
 NOTE: Turn the vacuum regulator valve counter-clockwise to increase the vacuum
 (differential pressure). The arrow on the vacuum regulator valve indicates an
 increase of pressure not vacuum.

 WARNING: MANUALLY HOLD THE VACUUM HEAD ASSEMBLY AGAINST THE AIRPLANE
 FUSELAGE DURING THE TEST. IF YOU DO NOT MANUALLY HOLD THE
 VACUUM HEAD ASSEMBLY, IT CAN FALL FROM THE FUSELAGE SURFACE
 DURING THE TEST. INJURY TO PERSONNEL OR DAMAGE TO EQUIPMENT
 CAN OCCUR.
 (f) Put the vacuum head assembly on the safety relief valve on the airplane and open the
 vacuum head assembly valve.
 SUBTASK 21-32-21-725-006

 (2) Do the test:
 (a) Adjust the vacuum regulator valve so the indication on the vacuum rate gage does not
 exceed 2.4 psi/minute.

RAM ALL 21-32-21

 D6-37569 Sep 25/2015

 (b) When the differential pressure gage shows 7.6 psid, adjust the vacuum regulator valve to
 increase the differential pressure in 0.05 psi increments.
 (c) Stop the increase of vacuum for 10 seconds between each increase of 0.05 psid.
 (d) Continue the intermittent vacuum increases of 0.05 psid until the safety relief valve
 opens.
 (e) Monitor the indication on the differential pressure gage when the valve opens.
 NOTE: The indication that the relief valve opens is seen on the differential pressure gage
 when the pressure starts to decrease or on the vacuum rate gage when the
 vacuum rate goes to zero.
 (f) Make sure the valve opens at a differential pressure of 8.01 to 8.35 psi (16.3 to 17.0
 inches of Hg).
 (g) Make sure the tubing connections are tight if the valve opens at a value that is too large.
 (h) Do these steps to make sure that the valve seat on the safety relief valve has fully closed:
 1) Adjust the vacuum regulator valve so the indication on the vacuum rate gage does
 not exceed 2.4 psi/minute.
 2) Make sure that you are able to increase the vacuum until the differential pressure
 gage shows 7.0 psid.

procedimento:

 EQUIPMENT.

 (g) Align the index mark on the sensor shaft with the centerline of the crank arm.

(1) The purpose of this test is to check the integrity of the bus transfer interlocks provided by the
 auxiliary contacts of the Main Power Circuit Breakers. Transfer times of approximately 8 to 12
 milliseconds indicate correct behavior of the interlock and the integrity of the associated
 airplane wiring. Transfer times of approximately 4 milliseconds would indicate the loss of the
 appropriate interlock due to either 1. a malfunction of the auxiliary contact in the contactor
 being transferred FROM or 2. a short in the associated wiring which bypasses the auxiliary
 contact.
 This condition by itself would not result in paralleling sources but if coupled with a contactor
 slow to drop out by an additional 4 milliseconds or more, paralleling would be expected.

 SUPPLY HAS AN EARTH GROUNDED NEUTRAL, THERE MUST NOT BE AN OPEN

 AIRPLANE. IF THE GROUND RETURN (NEUTRAL) CIRCUIT ON THE EXTERNAL
 POWER SUPPLY OR THE EXTERNAL POWER RECEPTACLE DOES NOT
 OPERATE CORRECTLY, REPAIR THE EXTERNAL POWER SUPPLY OR INSPECT
 THE EXTERNAL POWER RECEPTACLE NEUTRAL GROUND (PAGEBLOCK 24-41-

procedimento:
(1) If you use the External Power Receptacle in a dirty area too frequently, this will wear the
 receptacle pin and plug socket. This will cause too much heat and incorrect electrical
 connections.
 Corrosion or loose connections can also be the cause of the receptacle pins which become too
 hot. The connections are from the electrical conductors to the inner ends of the pins. Worn
 parts, too much heat and the result of the oxidation and corrosion will cause the pin and socket
 dimensions to change.
 (2) The external power receptacle contains four ac input pins that are 0.435 to 0.437 inch in the
 diameter. The receptacle also contains two dc control pins that are 0.310 to 0.312 inch in the
 diameter.
 The six pins are attached to a plastic base. The six pins have threads on the inboard ends, for
 the connection of the electrical cables. You cannot remove the pins for a replacement. Replace
 the damaged or smaller contact pins with a new support base which contains the six pins.
cuidados:

 WEAR GAGE IS A GO-NO-GO GAGE AND SHOULD NOT FIT OVER THE
 PIN. TOO MUCH FORCE ON THE PIN CAN CAUSE DAMAGE.
 1) Try to slide the wear gage set, SPL-1625 over the external power receptacle pins.

(1) The area for repair of decorative surfaces must be smaller than 100 in2 (64,516 mm2). If the

 vendors.

 paint with high-grade commercial standards.

SUBTASK 26-14-11-864-001

 NOTE: The screws are attached to the faceplate and cannot be removed.
 SUBTASK 26-14-11-034-003

 (3) Remove the faceplate from the smoke detector case.
 SUBTASK 26-14-11-034-005

 (4) Remove the two mounting screws which attach the smoke detector case to the ceiling bracket.
 SUBTASK 26-14-11-024-006

 (5) Remove the smoke detector and the ceiling bracket from the ceiling.
 SUBTASK 26-14-11-034-007

 (6) Disconnect the electrical connector.
 SUBTASK 26-14-11-034-008

 (7) Hold the smoke detector case and disconnect the lanyard from the rear of the smoke detector.

SUBTASK 26-14-11-434-020

 (1) Attach the lanyard from the ceiling bracket to the smoke detector case.
 SUBTASK 26-14-11-434-011

 (2) Put the ceiling bracket on top of the smoke detector.
 SUBTASK 26-14-11-434-012

 (3) Loosely tighten the two mounting screws on the smoke detector case.
 SUBTASK 26-14-11-434-013

 (4) Connect the connector to the smoke detector.
 SUBTASK 26-14-11-424-014

 (5) Put the smoke detector into the ceiling.
 SUBTASK 26-14-11-434-015

 (6) Push on the screws until the ceiling bracket moves into its position.
 SUBTASK 26-14-11-434-018

 (7) Tighten the screws which hold the ceiling bracket in its position.
 SUBTASK 26-14-11-434-017

 (8) Put the faceplate on the smoke detector.
 SUBTASK 26-14-11-434-016

 (9) Tighten the two faceplate screws.
 SUBTASK 26-14-11-864-019

 (10) Close the PASS & CREW CALL/LAV SMOKE DETECTOR circuit breaker on the P18-4 panel.
 SUBTASK 26-14-11-714-021

 (11) Do a test of the Lavatory Smoke Detection System (PAGEBLOCK 26-14-00/501).

SUBTASK 26-14-11-167-002

 (1) Use a medium nylon bristle brush, STD-3911 to remove the dust from the external surfaces of
 the smoke detector.
 SUBTASK 26-14-11-167-003

 (2) Use a lint-free cloth, G01043 to clean the smoke detector.
 SUBTASK 26-14-11-027-011

 WARNING: DO NOT DISASSEMBLE THE SENSOR CELL ASSEMBLY, DUE TO THE
 RADIOACTIVE MATERIAL CONTAINED WITHIN.
 (3) Do this task: Removal of the Lavatory Smoke Detector, TASK 26-14-11-004-009.
 SUBTASK 26-14-11-017-002

 (4) Move the lock release mechanism to remove the smoke sensor from the smoke detector
 assembly.
 SUBTASK 26-14-11-027-003

 (5) Put a screwdriver in the slot between the sensor cover and the body.

 26-14-11

 (6) Twist the screwdriver to release the cover lock.

 SUBTASK 26-14-11-167-008

titulo: Engine Fire Extinguisher Bottle Pressure Check
procedimento:
SUBTASK 26-21-11-786-001

 (1) Measure the pressure in the fire extinguisher bottle (referred to as the fire bottle).
 (a) Permit the bottle to get ambient temperature and use ambient temperature to find the
 pressure.
 (b) Find the higher pressure limit and the lower pressure limit from the fire bottle temperature
 that was measured and (Figure 601).
 (c) If there is a pressure gauge on the bottle, read the pressure gauge on the fire bottle.
 1) Compare the pressure in the fire bottle (read from the gauge) with the higher and
 lower pressure limits.
 2) Make sure the pressure in the fire bottle is more than the lower limit.
 3) Make sure the pressure in the fire bottle is less than the higher limit.
 a) If the pressure in the fire bottle is more than the higher limit, or less than the
 lower limit, replace the fire bottle with a serviceable fire bottle.

 (g) a bell cutout switch,

 bottle are on cards in the module.

procedimento:
(1) Before you adjust the trailing edge flaps, these checks must be satisfactory with the flaps in the
 up position:
 (a) The angular clearance between the upstops on the ballscrew yoke and the ballscrew nut
 must be 170 to 190 degrees (1/2 turn ±10 degrees) turn. If you made trim correction, the
 angular clearance can be 1/4 to 5/6 turn.
 (b) Adjustment of the flap transmissions is necessary if the angular clearance is more than
 the specified limits.
 (2) These checks must be satisfactory with the flaps in the 40-unit detent:
 (a) The clearances between the midflap trailing edge to the aftflap leading edge for the
 inboard ends (of the left and right flaps) and outboard ends (of the left and right flaps)
 must be equal.
 A tolerance of 0.05 inch is permitted.
 (b) Adjustment of the aftflap bellcrank clevis arm is necessary if the left and right flap
 clearances are not equal.
cuidados:

procedimento:
(1) When you install new cables, the initial cable tension must be two times the applicable values
 shown in Figure 501. After you operate the system 20 times, you must adjust the cable tension
 again to the correct values.
 (2) The aileron control wheels have a foil marker calibrated in units of the aileron trim. The foil
 markers are used by the flight crew only. Do not use the foil markers when you adjust or do a
 test of the aileron control system unless it is specified.
 (3) You must adjust the aileron trim control system before you do a check or adjust the aileron
 control system. The aileron trim control system is at the center when you can easily install or
 remove the rig pin A/S-15. To do this, operate the two trim switches at the same time (with
 airplane electrical power on) to supply power to the trim actuator.
 WARNING: MAKE SURE THAT PERSONS AND EQUIPMENT ARE CLEAR OF ALL CONTROL
 SURFACES BEFORE YOU SUPPLY HYDRAULIC POWER. AILERONS, RUDDERS,
 ELEVATORS, TRAILING EDGE FLAPS, LEADING EDGE FLAPS AND SLATS,
 SPOILERS, LANDING GEAR, AND THRUST REVERSERS CAN MOVE QUICKLY
 WHEN YOU SUPPLY HYDRAULIC POWER. THIS CAN CAUSE INJURY TO
 PERSONS OR DAMAGE TO EQUIPMENT.
 (4) The aileron and aileron trim control systems are correctly adjusted with these conditions
 (Figure 501):
 (a) Aileron Control Bus Cables ACBA and ACBB
 1) With the rig pin A/S-1A installed, the straightedge is on the top ends of the captain's
 and the first officer's control wheels (Figure 503).
 NOTE: One end of the first officer's control wheel must not be farther than 0.20 inch
 from the straightedge.
 2) The cable tension is as specified (Figure 501).
 3) If it is necessary, adjust the cables ACBA and ACBB in the lower nose compartment.
 (b) Aileron Control Cables AA and AB
 1) These are the results with the rig pins A/S-1, A/S-1A, and A/S-15 installed:

 (1) Do a test of the aileron control drum:
 (a) Use a torque wrench on the adapter to measure the force necessary to turn the captain's
 aileron control wheel clockwise and counterclockwise.
 NOTE: If the adapter is not available, put a tangent force to the captain's control wheel at
 a 6.5 inch radius.
 1) Turn the control wheel clockwise until the ailerons start to move.
 a) Make sure the necessary force is not more than 192 pound-inches torque or
 29.5 pounds.
 2) Continue to turn the control wheel to 20 degrees.
 a) Make sure the necessary force is not more than 200 pound-inches torque or
 33.8 pounds.
 3) Continue to turn the control wheel to 40 degrees.
 a) Make sure the necessary force is not more than 256 pound-inches torque or
 39.4 pounds.
 4) Continue to turn the control wheel to 75 degrees.
 a) Make sure the necessary force is not more than 310 pound-inches torque or
 47.7 pounds.
 5) Do steps 1) thru 4) again in the counterclockwise direction.
 (b) Turn the captain's control wheel more than 87 degrees counterclockwise from the neutral
 position.
 1) Make sure the left aileron moves up and the right aileron moves down in the
 specified limit (Figure 502).
 (c) Turn the captain's control wheel more than 87 degrees clockwise from the neutral
 position.
 1) Make sure the left aileron moves down and the right aileron moves up in the limit
 shown in Figure 502.

(1) This test gives instructions for a system check to make sure satisfactory of all adjustment
 specifications and performance of the elevator and tab control system. To do this test you must
 do the checks of these components:

procedimento:
