 (2) The inner pane is not structurally important. A deterioration in the visual quality of the inner
 pane is the only cause for its replacement.
 (3) Different types of window damage are specified below:
 (a) Crazing: A crazing is a number of very small cracks perpendicular to the surface of the
 plastic. Because of the very small width of the cracks, a crazing is not easy to see when
 you look directly at the surface. You can see a crazing by the reflection of the smooth
 surfaces of the cracks at different angles to the light.
 1) The routed edge of the window pane is the usual location for a crazing to occur. The
 routed edge usually has more contamination from solvents and other materials
 while it is cleaned or painted. The contamination can get into the clearance between
 the window pane and the frame and can soak into the seal. Also, the routed radius
 causes a stress raiser of near the maximum shear transfer.
 2) A crazing is usually caused by an incorrect installation. You can also cause a
 crazing if you accidentally apply materials which are not applicable for acrylic
 windows.
 3) A crazing in the radius of the routed edge (Figure 602) of an outer pane is more
 dangerous than that in the surface. As the crazing moves around the radius to the
 outer surface of the pane the crazing becomes less dangerous. This is because the
 stress level decreases. If there is a crazing at the intersection of the outer contour
 with the routed edge, there is not very much stress.
 (b) Crack: A crack has width which you can see when you look directly at the surface. A
 crack can become larger in any direction. The angle that the crack becomes larger,
 depends on the direction of the force. A crack in the stretched acrylic can have chevron or
 clamshell growth lines. A crack will become larger from a stressed area such as a scratch
 or a crazing (Figure 601).
 (c) Scratch: A scratch is the removal or movement of material from the surface of the window
 along a line. The depth and width of the scratch are usually small.

(1) The rework limits on the outer panes should be limited to the minimum thicknesses after
 rework as shown in (Figure 801).
 (2) When you polish or buff the window with your hand, you should use a circular motion of your
 hand and cover as large a portion of the window as possible. Start at the center of the pane
 and move out towards the edges. It is recommended that you use a clean lint-free cloth,
 G00834 for each step in the procedure. Superficial scratches can be removed by applying
 polish to a wet clean cloth and then rub the window. For minor scratches, it may be necessary
 to rub first with a lint-free cloth, G00834 and a fine buffing compound. A satisfactory buffing
 compound is Learok 884E compound, B00027. Finish polishing the window with one of the
 recommended polishes.
 (3) Machine polishing and buffing are recommended when the equipment and an approved
 operator are available. You must regulate the contact pressure and the wheel to prevent
 overheating the surface.
 (a) You can remove minor or superficial scratches by machine polishing or buffing with
 Learok 884E compound, B00027 buffing compound. If it is necessary, you can do some
 preliminary buffing with a stitched muslin wheel, STD-9596 and a buffing compound such
 as Learock S-30. Do this at a wheel surface speed of 3200 feet per minute.
 (b) Do the final high gloss polishing with Learok 884E compound, B00027. For this, use a
 loose open unstitched muslin wheel with spacers or a loosely stitched wheel, G50350 at
 a surface speed of 4200 feet per minute. To make spacers, remove all the muslin disks
 and reduce half of them to 1/2 the original diameter. Reassemble the wheel but alternate
 large disks with small ones. This type of wheel reduces heating due to friction.
 (c) Sometimes you can find an unsatisfactory condition at the edge of the buffed area. If you
 hold the window at the correct angle to the light, a very slight clouded margin can be
 seen.
 One cause of this condition is insufficient wheel speed. You can eliminate this problem by
 increasing the wheel speed or buffing the entire surface of the window.

titulo: Polish the Leading Edge Light Lens
procedimento:
(1) This procedure gives the task to polish the exterior surface of the lens on the left or right
 wingtip.
SUBTASK 57-21-11-160-001

 (1) Apply small amounts of NuShine II, Grade S compound, B50025 along the leading edge of the
 lens.
 (a) Use a pair of protective gloves, G50140.
 (b) Do only half of the length of the lens at a time, or the polish will become dry too soon.
 (c) Polish with a high quality paper towel, G50141 with light pressure only in a linear motion
 along the leading edge.
 NOTE: Use only plain white or natural color paper towels.
 NOTE: There will be a transition line, approximately 0.25 in. (6.35 mm) wide between the
 hazed surface and the undamaged clear surface. Do not try to polish this portion
 of the lens, a hard coat material remains on the lens and can not be polish out to
 a clear state.

 (2) Repeat the polish process; after the polish process is complete, use a clean soft cotton cloth,
 G50138 in order to achieve a final luster.

(1) This procedure gives the instructions that are necessary to operate the engine during cold
 weather conditions. These instructions give the information, techniques, and additional
 procedures to supplement the usual operation procedure.
 (2) During cold weather operation, you can prevent damage to the engine if you do these steps:
 (a) Use the inlet cover and the exhaust cover.
 (b) Make sure the rotors are not locked before you start the engine.
 (c) You must prevent or remove the snow and ice that can collect around the inlet cowl.
 (3) Ice formation in the engine inlet is one of the principal hazards during cold weather engine
 operation.
 (a) Snow that is blown into a cooling engine can become ice if it melts and freezes again.
 1) This ice formation can lock the rotor blades to the stator case.
 2) This ice formation can cover the surface of the rotor blades and cause the blades to
 become unbalanced.
 (4) Rain and high winds that cause a large temperature decrease in a small amount of time can
 cause the ice to form in the engine and lock the rotors.
 (5) Ice formation during engine operation can occur because of the large airflows and the suction
 at the engine inlet.
 (a) This is very dangerous during engine operation at high power settings and static
 conditions on the ground.
 (b) The suction action decreases the air pressure with a subsequent decrease in the air
 temperature.
 (c) The evaporative cooling and the temperature decrease from the suction causes the ice to
 form when the water droplets hit the spinner, fan blades, and guide vanes.
 (6) When the engine is not operated, there is a possibility of foreign object damage (FOD) or
 snow/rain ingestion for some conditions.
 (a) It is recommended that the engine inlet and exhaust covers are installed when it is
 practical and necessary.
 (b) It is recommended that the airplane is pointed into the prevailing wind when it is parked
 for a long time.
 (7) During heavy snowstorms, the engine must be shut down in forward thrust to prevent ice
 formation on the thrust reverser cascade vanes, blocker doors, and linkages.
 (8) Jet engines do not usually need to be preheated and reliable starts can be done with the usual
 start procedures.

titulo: Test No. 12 - Engine Diagnostic Run Test
procedimento:
(1) This task provides the instructions on how to evaluate engine parameters while the engine is
 installed on the airplane and to help isolate a possible faulty system.
 (2) This procedure tests the Main Engine Control (MEC) N2 Speed Governing System, Variable
 Geometry (VSV/VBV) System, Power Management Control (PMC) System and the Airplane
 Engine Control for possible system faults. This procedure is intended only as an additional tool
 to enhance troubleshooting, and is in no way intended to replace the fault isolation charts.
 (3) The engine diagnostic run can be performed before or after any static testing is done.
 (4) For this test, it is necessary to operate each engine at Low and High Idle, Part Power Trim, and
 Maximum Power Assurance power settings. Procedures for these tests should be performed
 according to the applicable AMM sections.
 (5) Use the diagnostic run data sheet for this test to record engine parameters (Figure 501).
 (6) The engine data for the Idle Speed, Acceleration, Part Power, and MPA tests can be collected
 in one continuous run before analysis.
 Or, the analysis and related corrective actions can be done after each power level check.
 (7) The Main Engine Control N2 Speed Governing System controls N2 speeds according to PS12,
 T2, and Power Lever Angle. Incorrect inputs to the MEC or internal faults in the MEC can
 produce throttle stagger, thrust shortfall, variation in engine dynamics or starting difficulties
 (8) The Variable Geometry System schedules variable stator vane (VSV) and variable bleed vane
 (VBV) positions according to N2 speed, CDP, and CIT inputs. The Variable Geometry System
 will affect the N1/N2 speed relationship and incorrect inputs from the associated components
 will change this speed relationship. Acceleration, throttle stagger and thrust short fall problems
 can result from Variable Geometry mis-scheduling
 (9) The PMC system schedules fan speed, N1, as a result of PS12, T12, and PLA inputs. The N1
 speed is controlled by changes made to N2 speed by varying current to the torque motor in the
 MEC. Faults with the PMC system can result in throttle stagger, N1/EGT transient overshoot
 during takeoff, or a thrust shortfall.
 (10) Engine VSV systems that have been dynamically rigged, can have a change to the N1/N2
 speed relationship that will prevent the use of variable geometry condition results. A visual
 check of the MEC rig plate for alignment will show that a dynamic rig has been performed.

titulo: Power Plant (Up to 10 Days - Serviceable and Not Serviceable Power Plant) Preservation
procedimento:
(1) This task provides the instructions on how to preserve the engine up to 10 days.
 (2) The power plant preservation procedures are for engines that are installed on-wing.
 Procedures for engines that are removed from the airplane are in the CFMI Engine Shop
 Manual, Section 72-00-00, Page 1201.
 (3) Preservation instructions give the recommended procedures as the minimum steps necessary
 to prevent unwanted liquid and materials in the power plant, corrosion, and atmospheric
 conditions during times of storage and no operation, or landing after an in-flight shutdown.
 (4) If preservation renewal is permitted, it gives the instructions for the renewal of the preservation
 period.
 (5) The procedures are different for different lengths of non-operation time, different types of
 preservation, and if the power plant is serviceable or not serviceable.
 NOTE: For this procedure, the definition of an engine that is serviceable and an engine that is
 not serviceable is as follows: A serviceable power plant is one that you can start; a
 power plant that is not serviceable is one that you cannot start.
 (6) Preservation procedures in this section are recommended as an aid to find the necessary
 precautions that you must do to give sufficient protection to the power plant from the elements
 during times of storage and no operation.
 (a) Power plant preservation is a flexible program that you can do in such a way which best
 agrees with the applicable weather and storage conditions.

 serviceable to do the preservation renewal procedures and monitor the schedule regularly to
 make sure that you did the necessary procedures before the expiration of preservation time.
 (8) You must examine the preservation of the power plant as the weather conditions and
 conditions of power plant protection change and do the procedures necessary to keep the

(1) This task provides the instructions on how to do an inspection on the engine vents and drains
 system.
 (2) This task also gives the inspection criteria for fluid leakage from the engine/strut drains and the
 action to stop the leakage if the leakage rates are more than the limits.
 (3) The leakage rates given in the tables are the threshold limits and the servicable limits from
 different engine drain sources and both limits apply to engines that are not operated and
 engines that are operated at all power settings.
 (4) If the leakage rate is more than the serviceable limit, a corrective action is required.
 (5) If the leakage rate is less than the threshold limit, no action is required.
 (6) If the leakage rate is more than the threshold limit, but less than the servicable limit, an engine
 run is recommended to determine whether the leak increases or decreases with an operational
 engine and to verify the leakage source.
 (7) If you find leakage, the amount of the leakage must be measured to find the appropriate
 action.
 (8) The drain source nomenclature in the tables is more complete than the drain nomenclature on
 the placards. The drain source numbers in the tables will agree with the drain numbers on the
 placards.

procedimento:
(1) This task provides the instructions for the two procedures on how to clean the engine gas path.
 (a) You can clean the gas path with detergent wash or with water rinse only.
 (b) If you wash an engine gas path with the detergent wash, you must also wash the engine
 with the water rinse.
 (c) For EGT margin recovery, the engine manufacturer recommends that you do an
 evaluation to determine the best method for the operator.
 1) Pure water (without cleaning agent) is effective in most conditions but is dependent
 on the engine's operating environment and the engine gas-path cleaning program
 done by the operator.
 2) Engine gas-path water cleaning with detergent provides the most effective method
 to clean the engine compressors. If detergent is used, it is necessary to follow strict
 application of the engine rinsing and bleed system cycling per the procedure. This
 prevents fumes in the cabin when the airplane goes back into service.
 a) It may be necessary to clean the engine more than once if initial results are
 not satisfactory.
 b) Considerations should be given to do an engine gas-path cleaning with
 detergent for the following conditions:
 <1> Organic debris or oil deposits are observed on compressor airfoils
 <2> The engine has less than 50 °F (10 °C) EGT margin left.
 (2) Make sure that you use water with no more than 500 ppm total solids, 25 ppm sodium plus
 potassium (Na + K), and with a PH of 6.0-8.0.
 (a) Potable water is usually sufficient.
 (3) A water flow of 5-6 gpm (19-23 liters per minute) is necessary at a temperature of more than
 40°F (5°C).
 (a) For the best results, increase the temperature of the water to 150-200°F (65-95°C).
 (b) Hot water at 150-200°F (65-95°C) will wash and clean the gas path the best.
 (4) An anti-freeze solution must be used when you wash or rinse an engine if the air temperature
 is below 40°F (5°C). Prepare the anti-freeze solution as follows:
 (a) Use rubber gloves, STD-1086 and safety glasses, STD-1137.

(1) This trim balance procedure is done for these conditions:
 (a) To decrease the fan or LPT vibration levels when they are equal to or more than 8 mils
 DA (double amplitude).
 (b) When, after the replacement or the repair of a fan blade, the correction is more than 236
 gram-inches (600 g-cm).
 (c) Do not use this procedure to balance the engine, if the FFCCV alternate accelerometer is
 connected to the AVM instead of the usual No. 1 bearing acclerometer. Use the analyzer
 method to balance the engine.
 (2) The trim balance procedures should decrease the vibration levels of the fan and the LPT to
 less than 4.0 units on the airborne vibration monitor (AVM) during a ground operation at all
 engine operation speeds.
 (3) When an engine is installed on the wing, after an overhaul or after a replacement of a
 significant number of fan blades, it is recommended that you first do a vibration survey
 (PAGEBLOCK 71-00-00/501).
 (a) If the result of this vibration survey is not satisfactory, you can do one of these methods to
 balance the engine:
 1) Do a 3-shot plot trim balance procedure or analyzer procedure to decrease the
 engine vibration level; or,
 2) Use this procedure to balance the engine with the AVM.

titulo: Airborne Vibration Monitoring (AVM) System - Operational Test
procedimento:
(1) This task is the operational test procedure for the airborne vibration monitoring (AVM) system.
 (2) The operational test consists of three parts as follows:
 (a) A self-test of the AVM signal conditioner.
 (b) A fault history check of the complete AVM system for faults external to the AVM signal
 conditioner from the recent flight(s).
 (c) An engine operation (one engine at idle) to check that the AVM system is operational.
 (3) You can use the operational test to make sure that the AVM signal conditioner operates after a
 component replacement.

 sensor only for the duration of the malfunction of the primary NOB vibration sensor.

 THRUST REVERSER. THE ACCIDENTAL OPERATION OF THE THRUST

 EQUIPMENT.
 (1) Do the deactivation procedure for the thrust reverser for ground maintenance

(1) This task provides the instructions on how to do a leak check of the engine starter.
 (2) The intent of this task is to detect major oil leaks that are the result of a maintenance error,
 such as a missing or severely damaged O-ring on the starter output shaft.
 (3) It is recommended that operators carefully monitor the oil consumption on flights following
 starter installation. Do a high power engine run (>70 % N1) if the oil consumption shows a
 sudden increase.
 (4) It is recommended that the starter oil tank be re-serviced prior to conducting the idle leak check
 (TASK 12-13-41-603-001 and TASK 12-13-41-603-014). This will ensure maximum operational
 time in case of a small oil leak .
